```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
read_result <- function(name) {
  readr::read_csv(paste0("results/", name, ".csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
}
summary <- read_result("data_summary")
comparisons <- read_result("rasmussen_comparisons")
approval_holdout <- read_result("approval_holdout")
show_result <- function(name, digits = 2) knitr::kable(read_result(name), digits = digits)
week_conflicts <- read_result("approval_week_checks") |>
  dplyr::filter(abs(discrepancy) > 5)
election_components <- read_result("election_components") |>
  dplyr::count(component)

```

# Models and validation

The original analysis plotted Rasmussen and other polls with separate smooth
curves. It did not estimate adjusted house coefficients. Its approval comparison
is strongly affected by differences in polling dates: the raw Rasmussen gap is
`r round(comparisons$original_raw_gap[1], 2)` percentage points, compared with
`r round(comparisons$time_adjusted_gap[1], 2)` after adjusting for time in a
descriptive spline regression. The quantities answer different questions;
the latter is not a correction to the former's arithmetic.

The original election plot pooled states and national polls. Geography is a
necessary comparison dimension, although adding geography to the time-adjusted
Rasmussen-versus-rest regression changes that particular McCain-support
coefficient only slightly. The comparison below uses 20-degree-of-freedom natural
splines and is distinct from the primary Bayesian models.

```{r comparisons, results='asis'}
show_result("rasmussen_comparisons")
```

## Quantities being estimated

| Analysis | Unit and outcome | Comparison | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Approval | Poll, Bush approval percentage | Other houses at comparable dates | Historical relative approval house effect |
| Election | Poll, McCain minus Obama percentage points | Other houses at comparable dates and geographies | Historical relative partisan-margin house effect |
| Sample-size sensitivity | Poll, same outcome with approximate sampling variance | Restricted to reported positive sample sizes | A different available-data sample and precision model |

The reference is the equal-weight mean of qualifying houses, separately for
each dataset. The reference mean is subtracted within every posterior draw,
propagating its uncertainty into all reported contrasts. Absolute accuracy
cannot be identified without an external opinion benchmark. Election-day
results would measure a different target from opinion months before voting.
The interpretation is associational: no intervention or random assignment
identifies the effects of particular polling practices.

## Data integrity

```{r data-summary, results='asis'}
summary |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-dataset, as.character)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-dataset, names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Value") |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = dataset, values_from = Value) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Original source files are unchanged. Row identifiers are the original CSV line
numbers, including the header. Explicit joins declare their cardinality, and
tests enforce row accounting and the signs and units of derived outcomes.

The election source has duplicate `n` headers. The first contains the reported
sample size and population text; the second is a derived numeric field. The
importer assigns distinct names and parses the source text.
`r summary$missing_sample_size[summary$dataset == "election"]` polls
report a population label without a sample size; their derived zero becomes
unknown. The national YouGov row reports 31,148 respondents in its text but
3,114 in its derived column. The text is retained as the source value; this is
an internal reconciliation, not independent verification of the original poll.

Election dates are reconstructed from the original single-day, same-month, or
cross-month strings. Derived years such as `208`, zero months, and conflicting
day fields are not used for estimation.
The approval week field also disagrees with recorded dates by more than five
weeks in `r nrow(week_conflicts)` rows, including a Rasmussen row differing by about a year.
The primary analysis gives precedence to dates; a sensitivity fit excludes
these conflicts. This tests the consequence of that precedence rule without
claiming independent verification of either source field.

Three election date strings run backwards and remain unresolved. Approval
exclusions comprise seven incomplete date intervals and two unverified
fieldwork intervals longer than 30 days. The latter are 44 and 239 days; using
their midpoints could misplace a poll by months. This explicit exclusion rule
does not establish the true dates. Exclusions are flagged in the cleaned data.
A sensitivity fit restores the two long intervals using their recorded midpoints
to show the consequence of excluding them.

Missing approval screen indicators and `(lv = 0, rv = 0)` are treated as
unknown because the file does not establish an adult-population definition.
Outcome categories such as `neither`, `unsure`, and `dk` may overlap; they are
not added together or recoded to zero. The margin uses the original percentages
without two-party normalization. The data contain no exact duplicate rows or
duplicate house/geography/fieldwork keys after cleaning. Overlapping fieldwork
is retained in the primary model and thinned in a sensitivity analysis.

House-name normalization trims whitespace and merges three spelling/order
variants: `StrategicVision (R)`, `Fox/Rasmussen`, and the reversed
Research 2000/DailyKos sponsor label. Different sponsors and internet/telephone
series otherwise remain separate. These labels are polling series, not a
verified corporate-family genealogy.

## Model specification

The response is centered at 50 for approval and zero for the election margin.
Both likelihoods use multivariate Student-t errors with an identity link.
House intercepts are normally distributed with an estimated scale. Polls within
a house and calendar fortnight form a block with scale matrix
`σ² I + τ² 11′`. Blocks are independent conditional on the model parameters.
Their covariance is the scale matrix multiplied by `ν / (ν - 2)`.
A shared normal shock and independent normal errors, divided by a common
chi-square scale within the block, give this distribution. The likelihood
integrates out the block shocks analytically; predictions draw them jointly.

The custom Stan density is checked against `mvtnorm` for correlated blocks,
independent observations, and heterogeneous known sampling variances. The common time trend uses a cubic B-spline with 60 basis columns
for approval and 15 for elections. Interior knots are evenly spaced over
fixed boundaries (2001–2009 for approval; 2007–2009 for elections). The first
basis column is omitted to identify the intercept. Basis coefficients have
normal priors with 20-point scale. Knots remain fixed for held-out prediction.

Approval also includes a level break on September 11, 2001. For fieldwork that
crosses that date, exposure is the fraction of recorded fieldwork days on or
after September 11, assuming uniform interviewing across those days. This
approximates the abrupt common change while keeping the smooth trend for other
movements; it is not a causal estimate of the event. Residual review of the
smooth-only pilot found large systematic overpredictions in several pre-event polls:
the spline had spread the later jump backwards. The explicit break addresses
that failure, and a smooth-only sensitivity fit shows its effect on house
contrasts.

![Approval trend around September 11](../figs/approval_break_check.png)

```{r break-check, results='asis'}
read_result("approval_break_predictions") |>
  dplyr::filter(midpoint < as.Date("2001-09-11")) |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(polls = dplyr::n(), rmse = sqrt(mean(residual^2)),
                   maximum_absolute_residual = max(abs(residual)), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The remaining large residual in this window is a CNN–USA Today–Gallup poll
recorded as September 8–11 with 51% approval. Uniform exposure assigns one
quarter of its interviews to September 11. The source does not supply interview
times or daily counts, so that approximation can overstate exposure to the
post-event shift. Its recorded dates and outcome are retained.

Basis-size and prior-scale sensitivities check the regularization of the time trend.

Election geography intercepts have normal priors. Geography deviations use
four natural cubic spline basis columns with interior knots at mid-2007,
early-2008, and mid-2008, and boundaries at early-2007 and early-2009.
Each coefficient has its own estimated across-geography scale; coefficients
are independent a priori. National polling is one geography, not an aggregate
imposed on state polls.

Normal prior scales are 20 percentage points for intercepts and unpenalized
coefficients, 5 for group scales, and 10 for the residual scale. Scale
parameters are constrained positive. Degrees of freedom follow two plus an
exponential distribution with rate 0.1. These priors are deliberately broad;
prior predictive checks quantify mass beyond percentage bounds. Student-t tails
allow unusual observations without deleting them. A continuous likelihood can
predict outside the logical bounds, so predictive behavior must be checked.

Each published fit uses four chains with at least 1,000 warmup and 1,000 retained
iterations per chain and maximum tree depth 13. Primary fits use
`adapt_delta = 0.99`. Approval fits use a dense Euclidean metric to accommodate
correlations among trend coefficients; election fits use a diagonal metric.
Supplementary fits start at 0.95, with 0.99 and longer
chains used when diagnostics require a retry. Publication
requires E-BFMI of at least 0.3 in every chain, no divergences or tree-depth hits,
R-hat at most 1.01, and bulk and tail
effective sample sizes of at least 400 for every reported house contrast.

```{r diagnostics, results='asis'}
for (dataset in c("approval", "election")) {
  cat("\n\n### ", dataset, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(show_result(paste0(dataset, "_diagnostics"), 3))
}
```

## Benchmarks, support, and sensitivity

Unpooled least-squares benchmarks control for geography-by-month cells
(month alone for approval). A bipartite house/cell graph identifies connected
comparison components before estimating contrasts. Benchmark estimates are
centered within connected components and are point-estimate diagnostics;
they do not supply the headline uncertainty intervals. All approval houses
are connected. The election comparison graph has one main component with
`r max(election_components$n)` houses and `r sum(election_components$n == 1)` isolated houses; those isolated comparisons rely on the
Bayesian model rather than within-cell contrasts. Rank, condition number,
and maximum leverage are saved alongside them. High leverage and weak overlap
limit what the data can establish even when the Bayesian sampler converges.
The overlap flag is descriptive: a qualifying house is labeled `supported`
when at least half its polls share a geography-month cell with another house,
and `limited overlap` otherwise. This threshold does not validate the time
trend or selection assumptions.

For Rasmussen, the month-cell benchmark and the primary smooth-trend model
compare as follows. Their time controls differ, and only the Bayesian model
partially pools house effects.

```{r benchmark-comparison, results='asis'}
lapply(c("approval", "election"), function(dataset) {
  read_result(paste0(dataset, "_houses")) |>
    dplyr::filter(house == "Rasmussen") |>
    dplyr::select(house, estimate, lower, upper) |>
    dplyr::left_join(
      read_result(paste0(dataset, "_benchmark")) |>
        dplyr::select(house, benchmark),
      by = "house", relationship = "one-to-one"
    ) |>
    dplyr::mutate(dataset = dataset, .before = 1)
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The sensitivity tables below show Rasmussen to make specification changes
easy to inspect. Complete results for every house are in the CSVs.
Each subset is compared with the primary fit recentered on the same available
reference houses. Changing the sample can change the estimand. The McCain-only
outcome differs from the margin, so its coefficient difference is not a
stability statistic.

The influential-house exclusions are:

```{r omitted-houses, results='asis'}
lapply(c("approval", "election"), function(dataset) {
  read_result(paste0(dataset, "_sensitivity")) |>
    dplyr::filter(omitted_house != "none") |>
    dplyr::distinct(specification, omitted_house) |>
    dplyr::mutate(dataset = dataset, .before = 1)
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  knitr::kable()
```

An exclusion of Rasmussen has no Rasmussen coefficient to report; its effects
on the remaining houses appear in the complete sensitivity file.

```{r sensitivity, results='asis'}
for (dataset in c("approval", "election")) {
  cat("\n\n### ", dataset, "\n\n", sep = "")
  x <- read_result(paste0(dataset, "_sensitivity")) |>
    dplyr::filter(house == "Rasmussen") |>
    dplyr::select(
      specification, estimate, lower, upper, primary_estimate, difference, n_polls, n_reference
    )
  print(knitr::kable(x, digits = 2))
}
```

The next table reports the largest change among reference houses in each
specification. These are differences between posterior means, not tests of
statistical significance. The McCain-support outcome is excluded because it
uses a different scale from the margin.

```{r sensitivity-all-houses, results='asis'}
lapply(c("approval", "election"), function(dataset) {
  read_result(paste0(dataset, "_sensitivity")) |>
    dplyr::filter(reference, specification != "mccain") |>
    dplyr::group_by(specification) |>
    dplyr::slice_max(abs(difference), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    dplyr::ungroup() |>
    dplyr::transmute(dataset = dataset, specification, house, difference)
}) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The sample-size variant uses Gaussian observation error with approximate
simple-random-sampling variances plus estimated residual error. For the margin,
the variance is `10000 * (p_mccain + p_obama - (p_mccain - p_obama)^2) / n`;
candidate shares from the same sample are not independent. Survey design
effects and weighting are unavailable, so these are not known true standard
errors. The primary model avoids treating these approximations as exact.

## Prediction and simulation checks

```{r prediction, results='asis'}
for (dataset in c("approval", "election")) {
  cat("\n\n### ", dataset, "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(show_result(paste0(dataset, "_predictive_checks")))
  print(show_result(paste0(dataset, "_posterior_bounds"), 6))
  print(show_result(paste0(dataset, "_prior_checks")))
  print(show_result(paste0(dataset, "_residual_dependence")))
  print(show_result(paste0(dataset, "_holdout")))
}
```

The approval forward holdout performs poorly: RMSE is
`r round(approval_holdout$rmse, 1)` points, mean interval width is
`r round(approval_holdout$mean_interval_width_95, 1)` points, and nominal 95%
intervals cover `r round(100 * approval_holdout$predictive_coverage_95, 1)`% of
later polls. Unobserved future spline coefficients are governed by their priors,
so this specification does not provide a useful forecast over that long gap.
This failure limits predictive use; retrospective house comparisons are assessed
separately with the month-cell benchmarks and specification checks above.

Dark curves below show observed distributions; light curves show 40 replicated
datasets. Approval is centered at 50; the election outcome is the partisan margin.

![Approval predictive distributions](../figs/approval_predictive.png)

![Election predictive distributions](../figs/election_predictive.png)

The election replications have a lower central peak than the observed margins.
This is a remaining mismatch even though the mean, spread, and extremes are
broadly reproduced.

Posterior predictive intervals above summarize replicated dataset statistics,
not uncertainty about a single observation. Residual correlations use consecutive
polls within the same house and geography, restricted to the stated time gaps,
and distinguish pairs within and between model blocks. Positive correlation
between fortnights indicates dependence beyond the fitted block structure.
The four-week-block sensitivity tests the consequence of allowing longer shared
shocks. It cannot establish that all dependence has been captured; uncertainty
intervals remain conditional on the assumed error structure.
Blocked validation trains on the earliest 80% of midpoint dates and predicts
the remaining dates, integrating new house-period effects. Rows from geographies
absent in training are excluded from validation and counted explicitly.
Polls whose house-fortnight already appears in training are also excluded and
counted: predictions draw new error blocks, so these partially observed blocks
are outside the validation target. Long extrapolation
from a smooth trend can fail even when within-period house contrasts are useful;
these models are not offered as forecasting systems. Predictive simulations use
separate fixed seeds by dataset and stage, so running the datasets separately
or together gives the same summaries from the same saved fits.

```{r simulations, results='asis'}
read_result("simulation") |>
  dplyr::group_by(reference) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    contrasts = dplyr::n(), coverage = mean(covered),
    rmse = sqrt(mean(error^2)), mean_error = mean(error), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Simulations run the same model interface and posterior centering on known house
effects. They include strongly unequal geographic coverage, a sparse house,
missing sample sizes, and shared Gaussian house-period shocks with independent
Student-t noise. This deliberately differs from the fitted block Student-t
likelihood and provides a limited misspecification check. Ten simulated datasets
provide a basic recovery and interval-coverage check, not precise calibration
or evidence that every real-data assumption is correct. Per-replication sampler
diagnostics are saved in [simulation_diagnostics.csv](../results/simulation_diagnostics.csv).
